queries.q: Blackwell architecture compute capability numbering sm_100 sm_101 sm_120 sm_121 which GPUs map to which compute capability
queries.excerpt: From CUDA 13.0, the Blackwell SM101 for Thor GPUs is renamed to SM110.
queries.claim: gpu_profile.rs:520 `BLACKWELL_MIN_CC = 120` with the predicate `cc >= 120` at :512 is documented as identifying 'Blackwell'. This requires every Blackwell part to have cc >= 120.

queries.q: compute capability 10.0 Blackwell data center GPU B100 B200 versus compute capability 12.0 GeForce Blackwell architecture table
queries.excerpt: Note: The NVIDIA Blackwell SM100 architecture used in the datacenter products has a different compute capability than the one underpinning NVIDIA Blackwell GeForce RTX 50 series GPUs (SM120). As a result, kernels compiled for Blackwell SM100 architecture with arch conditional features (using `sm100a`) are not compatible with RTX 50 series GPUs.
queries.claim: `select_prefill_path(cc, env)` treats `cc >= 120` as equivalent to 'the GPU is Blackwell', and the serialized `reason` field emits the literal string "blackwell default" on that basis.

queries.q: cuBLAS workspace requirements when capturing cuBLAS calls into a CUDA graph, cublasSetWorkspace and stream capture performance
queries.excerpt:
| NVIDIA Blackwell Architecture (sm10x) | 32 MiB |
| NVIDIA Blackwell Architecture (sm12x) | 32 MiB |
queries.claim: Same claim as above, cross-checked against a non-CUTLASS source: NVIDIA's own cuBLAS table names BOTH sm10x and sm12x as 'NVIDIA Blackwell Architecture', so a `cc >= 120` test excludes the sm10x half of Blackwell.

queries.q: family-specific architecture features sm_100f sm_121f compute capability 12.1 binary compatibility across Blackwell family
queries.excerpt: Beginning with devices of Compute Capability 10.0, some architecture-specific features are common to devices of more than one compute capability. The devices that contain these features are part of the same family and these features can also be called *family-specific* features.
queries.claim: The diff assumes one architecture family maps to one contiguous compute-capability range that an inequality can express (`cc >= 120`, plus tests asserting cc 119 is 'just below Blackwell' and cc 130 is Blackwell).

queries.q: compute capabilities appendix table listing architecture names Turing 7.5 Ampere 8.0 Ada 8.9 Hopper 9.0 Blackwell 10.0 12.0
queries.claim: gpu_profile.rs:713-717 asserts the boundary as 'cc 119 is a discrete part and keeps the fast path'; generate_batched_streaming.rs:1294 lists 75/80/86/89/90/119 as 'discrete GPUs' that keep batched prefill. This presumes nothing real exists between 90 and 120.

queries.q: asynchronous concurrent execution kernel launch returns control to host thread before device completes the work
queries.excerpt: The application is then free to perform other tasks at the same time as the originally dispatched operation. When the final results of the initially dispatched operation are needed, the application must perform some form of synchronization to ensure that the operation in question has completed.
queries.claim: generate_2.rs:297-303 and :396-400 measure prefill with a host clock (`Instant::now()` / `elapsed()`) and store it as `last_phase_timings.prefill_ms`, the numerator §7.2 gates `prefill_ratio` on. A host-clock span only measures device work if the span ends after a synchronization.

queries.q: cudaMemcpy is a synchronous API that enqueues work to the legacy stream and synchronizes on it before returning
queries.excerpt: It is therefore also invalid to call synchronous APIs in this case. One example of a synchronous APIs is `cudaMemcpy()` which enqueues work to the legacy stream and synchronizes on it before returning.
queries.claim: Verification of the timing claim above: the serial prefill loop ends in `forward_gpu_resident` (uses.rs:117), which downloads logits to the host; the batched path ends in `prefill_eager`, which calls `self.stream.synchronize()` (prefill.rs:527) before returning. Both timed spans therefore close after a synchronizing operation, so `prefill_ms` does measure device work.

queries.q: stream capture prohibited operations: querying or synchronizing a capturing stream is invalid, cudaStreamIsCapturing capture status legacy default stream
queries.excerpt: It is invalid to synchronize or query the execution status of a stream which is being captured or a captured event, because they do not represent items scheduled for execution.
queries.claim: executor_api.rs:479 `graph_config()` reports captured-graph state by reading HOST-side maps (`batched_decode_graphs.keys()`, `prefill_graphs.keys()`, `decode_graph.is_some()`), not by querying a stream or graph object. The prohibition on querying a capturing stream therefore does not apply; the readout is safe.

queries.q: CUDA graph kernel node parameters are fixed when the graph is instantiated; host-side branches are not re-evaluated on graph launch, use cudaGraphExecKernelNodeSetParams to change them
queries.excerpt: Updates take effect the next time the graph is launched, so they do not impact previous graph launches, even if they are running at the time of the update. A graph may be updated and relaunched repeatedly, so multiple updates/launches can be queued on a stream.
queries.claim: graphed_capture.rs:397 caches the env-driven graph decision in a `OnceLock` and prefill.rs:22 caches `PREFILL_GRAPH`/`CUBLAS_PREFILL` likewise, on the stated ground that a mid-run env change must not make the report momentary. Under graph replay the kernel actually executed is the one recorded in the graph, so an env re-read could not change it anyway; caching makes the report agree with the device.

queries.q: CUDA graphs reduce CPU kernel launch overhead by submitting the whole graph in a single launch operation
queries.excerpt: By creating a CUDA graph that encompasses a workflow that will be launched many times, these overhead costs can be paid once for the entire graph during instantiation, and the graph itself can then be launched repeatedly with very little overhead.
queries.claim: graphed_capture.rs:415-425 and gpu_profile.rs GraphConfig claim the graphed and eager decode paths differ by roughly 5.6 ms of kernel-launch overhead per token, and that a receipt must therefore state which one ran. The docs support the mechanism (launch-overhead elimination) but state no magnitude.

queries.q: cudaMemGetInfo API gets free and total device memory
cuMemGetInfo free and total memory in bytes available to the current CUDA context on the device
cudaMemGetInfo returns free and total memory of the device including allocations by other processes and contexts
memory management API to query free device memory, driver reserved memory and fragmentation caveats
CUDA context creation reserves device memory; memory available for allocation is reduced by the context and by other processes sharing the GPU
how often should an application query free device memory, overhead of memory info queries in a performance critical loop
queries.excerpt: The`cudaMemPoolAttr*MemHigh` attributes are watermarks recording the max value achieved by the respective `cudaMemPoolAttr*MemCurrent` attribute since last reset.
queries.claim: executor_api.rs:452-470 `sample_vram_used()` derives `used = total - free` from `context.memory_info()` and folds it into an atomic high-water mark reported as `used_peak_bytes` / `used_now_bytes` under a struct documented as 'What this process can honestly say about its VRAM' (gpu_profile.rs VramReport). No authority was found stating that free/total from a memory-info query is attributable to the calling process; the driver's own documented per-process high-water mechanism is the mem-pool watermark, not a free-memory delta. NOT contradicted, but unverified: on a shared GPU `used_now`/`used_peak`/`preload_delta_bytes` include other processes' allocations and context overhead.

NVIDIA GB10 Grace Blackwell superchip DGX Spark compute capability sm_121 unified coherent memory
cuModuleLoadData and cuModuleGetFunction error when the requested kernel function is not present in the loaded module
PTX instruction dp4a four-way dot product target ISA notes requires sm_61 or higher
queries.excerpt: * A new `dp4a` instruction which allows 4-way dot product with accumulate operation.
queries.claim: gpu_profile.rs:16 documents the Legacy Q4K variant as 'no DP4A. Fallback for sm < 7.5' and :119 computes `has_dp4a = major > 7 || (major == 7 && minor >= 5) // sm_75+ (Turing)`. dp4a was introduced in PTX ISA 5.0, the version that added sm_60/sm_61/sm_62 targets — i.e. long before sm_75.

queries.q: __dp4a integer dot product intrinsic minimum compute capability 6.1 support for 8-bit integer dot product
queries.claim: Target ISA note for the dp2a/dp4a dot-product-accumulate family: sm_61 or higher, not sm_75. This is the authority for the `has_dp4a` cutoff and for the graphed_capture.rs:465 assertion that cc 86 is a 'pre-DP4A cc'.

queries.q: cuBLAS workspace CUDA graph capture cublasSetWorkspace performance regression workspace-free algorithms
queries.excerpt: Too small value of `workspaceSizeInBytes` may cause some routines to fail with `CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED` error returned or cause large regressions in performance.
queries.claim: prefill.rs:161-163 (now hoisted into `prefill_graph_enabled`) states that 'cuBLAS uses workspace-free algorithms during graph capture, which are 7x slower than eager cuBLAS'. The docs confirm that workspace starvation causes large cuBLAS performance regressions, but state no capture-specific algorithm substitution.

findings.failure_scenario: CI cannot complete because the property_tests target is not in the default-run packages (the workspace root), breaking the hardcoded cargo test command in ci.sh.
findings.summary: scripts/ci.sh step 4 fails because `cargo test --test property_tests` fails with 'no test target named property_tests in default-run packages'.
findings.disposition: agreed, pre-existing and out of scope: scripts/ci.sh is byte-identical on origin/main and reachable only via Makefile:777; filed as paiml/aprender#2852

findings.failure_scenario: The measurement harness sends a request with `ignore_eos: true`, but `apr serve` ignores it. The generation stops early on EOS, returning fewer tokens than `n_predict`. The harness then fails the run under PP-28 because `completion_tokens != n_predict`.
findings.summary: `apr serve` silently drops `ignore_eos` during deserialization because `ChatCompletionRequest` in `crates/apr-cli/src/commands/serve/types.rs` lacks the field.
findings.disposition: agreed for the SafeTensors route (serve/safetensors.rs mounts the handler that deserialises into the field-less type; files untouched by this PR); not the measured route — the GGUF/realizar route honours ignore_eos (PERF-039) and every witness slot completed n_predict tokens; filed as paiml/aprender#2853

findings.failure_scenario: A batch of size M with staggering will call in_flight.enter() M times initially, then again for each staggered prompt popped from pending_joins, reporting up to 2*M - 1 concurrent requests for a batch that never exceeded M slots. Conversely, recycled slots from rx in PMAT-074 never call enter(), under-counting actual concurrency. This breaks the PP-24 concurrent ladder derivation by overstating the peak_in_flight.
findings.summary: Double counting of staggered joins artificially inflates the in_flight_now metric in cuda_batch_scheduler.
